speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: This conversation with Nellie Olsen-Johanson took place in the McConnell Mansion in Moscow, Idaho on June 22, 1978. The interviewer is Rachel Foxman.

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Gather bark, sap of the bark, you know, the inside for flour. They dry that and grind flour and mix it with what little flour they have and potato flour. I said potato flour, I never heard of it. This is another thing that you should know. So they fixed this mill for potato flour and used the potato flour with this bark for bread. In Sweden. In Sweden. So now when Ed and I went out on the farm, we raised potatoes and there was no price for the potatoes. The potatoes were down 25 cents a sack, a hundred, and we had to pay that much for the burlap for the sack. We couldn't afford to sell the potatoes, so we buried them as much as we could. Well I said, are they going to lay to rot? Grandpa and I got along just great because we both felt adventurous. We were like, what can we do? Well Grandpa says, I think we can do something about it.

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: What… i said, well you know in Sweden when we were poor, we made a potato mill. Oh, a potato mill. Well yes, he said, we made a potato mill. It's a lot of work to it. And we made a grater's and by hand. My mother, he said, would sit and grate these potatoes into water. And they starch from the potatoes in the fine grating, which settled in the bottom in the water. So they take that off. You probably noticed how the starch in potatoes is gone. So we'd stay there, put it out on cloth and let it dry. And then we'd take a roller and roll it. And it was flour. Oh, I said, why can't we do that? Well yes, he says. So Ed, you know, was quite inventive. He invented one of the first heavy duty grease guns for cats. Which he got a good price. At that time it was a good price. But now it's nothing. So when he said, you know, he got this money, he said, well this is easy money made so that we're not going to spend it. No, I said, put it aside and sit on it. So he went and bought a school bond. You know, a 20 year school bond. And it was small interest and all that. Well now that school bond is due in September. And we have drawn that interest off it in 20 years. It doesn't just feel bad, but he couldn't be here till, and that was just $5 ,000. You know, on that school. So he made a little dividend on that, 4 % you can say on that school bond. But anyway, then Ed come in on this and we made a potato mill up there on the farm. Up here in North. He went down to the mill and took one of the pulleys, a wood pulley. It was a smaller pulley. And put a shaft on it, built a scaffold kind of there that he put this on. And took a sink, or yeah, it was a big sheet. And grabbed us and found holes in there with a big nail, you know, so they made it greater. He put it on the soft, on the end of the stump, you know, where the nail would go down through easily. I didn't know what, I thought it was straight wood, it wouldn't make any difference. But he said, oh yes, it makes it easier. Nail goes easier down in the top of the stump, he says, than it does on the straight board. So he made this thing. So then Ed took this thing and wrapped it over this pulley. They took down from the mill, nailed it onto that real gun. And took the old saw, wood saw motor, gas motor, and put it on, connected on to this pulley. And made a hopper so that we could put the potatoes in. Okay, now I had to wash them, get the eyes out of them so they couldn't see. So that I'd learn from them. And the, oh, I laughed and I just ran into hysterics. We put the potatoes in this hopper and when you start the mill, it's got potatoes flying all over from the hopper because the speed was too fast, you see the grain. So they'd cut the speed down a little bit. And we'd do the hopper and put a lid on when we put the potatoes in there. And then let that run down into tubs of water, the grating underneath the hopper. And there we started our little potato mill. And I washed the potatoes with flour and soldered down here to the stores, to Christine, took some to Moscow. Fifty cents a pound for the potato starch. So we averaged up, we got to put in 75 cents a sack for the potatoes by doing all that work.

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Who would do that now? But you can get by with it if you have to. Say that you were really hard up. And if you have potatoes or anything, you can utilize it some way. This is all, you know, good education to me to know these things, just little things. And another thing that was, I learned from my folks and his mother, I made butter. I turned, but we had three cows and I turned and I was so same with the cream, we couldn't afford to use it. So I could take it down here and trade it for groceries. But the, you know, in the winter the cream got so pale and the butter roll would look so sickening, just like lard. So grandma said, it smells, oh she says, in Sweden we did something to that. Take a carrot and grind it and then strain it to a fine cloth, to a linen cloth, put that in the cream and when you turn the new butter it will have color. And I did, and it turned down.

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: You know for a while we got this margarine butter in, they couldn't put the coloring in, they had to put it in a little bubble, I call it. So you had to rework that and put that coloring in. But I used just carrot, natural fruit, because it had.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Why couldn't they color that margarine originally? Why did they have to give color to help it?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: In the law… and I had to go and get, to the state to get a permit, not a permit, but have butter papers stamped with ounces of butter I put on it. And I still had them in my scrapbook left over some months. So you just couldn't take it to the store and just sell it, you had to have papers for No, I had to have that on there. Food control.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: What year was that?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: That was in 19, let's see 1918, 1917, 1918.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Because they didn't used to make people do that did they?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: No, but that came in then. It was alright. So they knew who had made the butter, knew where it come from, which was fine too. Right, right. And it's been a benefit to me, even being in Alaska on that. Because I had to take Crisco when we was about to camp. Because we had a lot of the Crisco for butter. And I'd salt it. And we had carrots, so I just made carrot and put it in so it was yellow. So I called it margarine.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Did it work?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: It worked, yes, sure it worked. Just took Crisco. With it I let it cool. But I called it soft butter. Of course it got pretty hard staying near the cold. But I said this is soft butter, get it? So those things, you know, need. It's the need that makes inventions and ideas. And then the two up there, we bought quite a bit of mayonnaise dressing. Because that already had the eggs in it. It was cheaper to make it, the mayonnaise from the eggs up there. One year, we had quite a bit, but it got cold. And when mayonnaise freezes, it separates. The oil goes up and it's so hard to get it back out with. No beater, you have to do by hand. So I thought, my gosh, what am I going to do? I've got to use this or something. So I got the idea of making a cake. And I tried it, and I made sure, and I made sure. And finally I perfected it. And I sent it in and I got $35. Sending that in to the mayonnaise company, making cake out of it. I still have the papers that I sent in.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: What kind of cake would you make?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Chocolate cake. See, I took one cup of mayonnaise.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Separated or the stuff that you beat back together?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: No, just separated. I baited it up. Because it has the eggs and it has the oil. And took one cup of sugar and I whipped the daylights out. So the sugar would melt. Count them in, yes. Then I made sure I had two cups of flour with this. And with this frozen mayonnaise, I wasn't too sure whether baking powder would do it. But I used both. Then a teaspoon of the baking powder and a half of the soda. And mix that together. And I put this all into the flour mixer and tasted it because the mayonnaise already had salt in it. So I had to salt it a little bit. Well, I just did this all together. Then I took three-fourths of a cup of just warm water. And beat it all together. And melted chocolate. So I used coco. So I used about half a cup, a little more coco. And mixed all together. And I said, now whatever comes out will be. We'll see. I'd just like to go with my receipt if I got any. Paid it in the pan. And it come out and it was all right. But it wasn't just perfect. So I worked on it again. And now I just got a pan. But I got the nation's out.

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: So I said, why don't you send that recipe in? For a... On my invention papers. So I thought, well, I'm going to send it in. I'll just send it in because it's going to cost me, I think, five dollars. To register this recipe. Well, I got thirty-five dollars out of it. I still have my receipt.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: The recipe that you'd send to the mayonnaise people?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes… but I sent it in so I'd get recognition, see, as being the first one. A number. I sent it in first and then sent that number into them. Into the mayonnaise people afterwards. Then I got sent the thirty-five dollars from the mayonnaise people. That's pretty clever. I should have probably brought that on, but I haven't at home. I have a scrapbook. This is what Dorothy Dyer says. Oh, everything she looked at, they should have yourself interest. But I don't know, it's just old memories by me.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: But it's so different than how we live now.

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Isn't it? You get along with what you have. And you change things like what you have. And like out there, you've got to compromise on something. And like all the boys often love pumpkin pie. Well, we were unsure of pumpkin pie. I just, you know, couldn't make it. So I thought, my gosh, I'm going to try something. So we had carrot. No, I had a lot of beans cooked up. And they were getting kind of, that's kind of getting old. So I thought, well, I'm going to try something. I'm going to take and strain out some beans. And I'm going to use them instead of pumpkin. And I got strained a lot and I made the same as it's spiced, but a little bit more. And it worked all right, but it did have a different taste to it. So one of the boys says, Nellie, said, what happened to the pumpkin pie? He said, it don't taste like it. No, I said, that's the pumpkin salt.

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: And it was beans. So now, oh, they wrote up some, I have several articles up there that different ones have written. And so they got a bang out of this. So they wrote this up in the paper, you know. I have the same kind of thing because they're kind of funny, but corny to you. I think it's so interesting. Like you said, you had to be clever back then to be able to survive. Yes, you had to think. I don't know if they know how to make a fire in the wind stove anymore. You know, it's kind of sad to me. Because to me, I don't know if I have something, if I have flour in the bin or sugar in the sugar box. Or say some butter and bar duck. I could make something out of it in a hurry. You know, just to do it. Or if you have cereal of any kind. And just, of course, being interested in food and cooking. And you know the value in different foods. How you can combine them. That's the secret, I think.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Do you think a lot of it had to do with because you were in remote areas?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes. A great deal that you didn't have to do that. And started, you know, with the parents in remote. Like potatoes now, for instance, you can fix it up in so many different ways. That it's amazing. You think, now, take, we used to start with cowboys. And stuff, you know, potatoes, cowboys, mashed potatoes. You take fresh potatoes if you have. You wouldn't even peel them. Just wash them out real good and grate them. On a little coarser, not the real fine grater, but that. And just grate them on. Then you take bacon, you fry your bacon. And you just pour them right on top of the bacon. Spread it on in the pan. And you have a whole meal right in there. Try it sometimes. Take bacon, fry the bacon. Grate your potatoes with the peelings and all. Put it on top of the bacon. A little salt and a little pepper. And it don't take much cooking. You got the starch, you got everything right in there. Turn it over and it makes a good meal when you're hungry. Just that simple thing. And like I said, you can make the starch out of it. I made all my puddings up when I was on the farm. Fruit puddings, you know. Raspberry juice and then you use potato starch, which is finer than the corn starch. And you could go down here and try to buy potato starch. You pay a fortune for it. And then you can just make it yourself. By grating in the finer, not too fine grater, but when you get in water the starch settles. And then you can use the grating for cooking, besides. So you can utilize it in many, many different ways. And this has, this is my education from my parents and from these older people has been more benefit to me than my book work, than reading the recipes and all this. Of course I think it's very interesting to see the different combinations they have come up with in food, through experiments, which you've got to expect to do. But for the old fundamental part, in the beginning, when this wasn't available, you had to come up with something. Like you were saying your father-in-law used the bark from the trees. Yes, the inner bark. Just peeling, grinding and grounding. And they grounded with the stones. And this was interesting when I was in Sweden. And I didn't know this either about my father-in-law. He had a flour mill there, set up a flour mill, when he got to, you know, so he could, you know, after the famine and all that. And a saw mill he had there. So he ground the barley and oats and wheat that they raised. And there they had gone and got these big stones and carved them out, and two stones around the flour. And now when I was in Sweden, I went out and here one of those stones were still laying where the mill burned. That big stone, I said, that's an odd stone, I told Ed's cousin. Oh, he said that's just a stone that was left after the old flour mill that Johanson had. And that was very interesting to me too. And then the dam, they had a big dam there for a pond, you see, for the flour mill and the saw mill. I said, this dam is so interesting, you know, this way. Oh, he said Johanson built that too.

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: You mean Grandpa Johanson? Yes, and your husband's father… that was there… so I went down and I took and knocked off a piece of stone off of the dam. So I had that. I brought that so that I was going to give it to John, Ed's brother. But I hadn't gotten that far. Now I don't know if he needs it because he's 96 years old. But it'd be interesting. It'd be interesting for him.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: What brought your father-in-law over to the United States?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Adventure.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Not the Depression. No, not the... I mean the famine.

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Well, no, after the famine, he got, so he went ahead and he made a little money. He went into logging because there's a lot of timber in Sweden. And saw milling. And he had 600 mills working on there. So he was pretty well to do this and I didn't know that either. I didn't know nothing about them. I thought he was just a lumberjack out here, you know, on the farm. Like the rest of them. But no, he was adventurous. And the dentist. But then after the farm burned, then a friend of his, or a relative, moved out to Minnesota. So when they wrote, that's when he decided then after the mill burned to go to Minnesota. But as I could see, he would have been a wealthy man if he'd stayed right there in Sweden. He would have been just... had more soul than... But he was pretty adventurous there too. Seems like everybody liked him. You know, when you're a kid, you don't pay attention to things. You know, when I was... See, I was only 19 years old when I married. And then I was just a kid. But of course, now, they're very younger than that. So it was just the adventure, just the idea of coming out to a new country. That was it.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Can you remember what year that was that he came out?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: No, I can't. But I could find out. It was in the 1800s. It was before the railroad went down through to Lewiston. From Moscow here. Before that. And I think Poland was the closest railroad at that time. So Moscow wasn't much either.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Would it be around the 1870s, would you imagine?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: There should be a record of it. A historical record. Either at the university or at the courthouse. Or when the railroad was put in at that time. Or when Vollmer... Vollmer was Troy at that time. But it was changed because Vollmer was too greedy. That's the thing. You know, when the farmers, they lost their home, a few of them. And that made them... Vollmer shouldn't be the name of Troy. They weren't changed. That was the reason Grandpa said that. But he had a sawmill right down the middle of Troy, which is Troy. That's how he started out. Vollmer. So, the way he talked about it, it couldn't be somebody else too. That had the sawmill. That should be a record of it. From that beginning. Now, I was with Mary Driscoll.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Isn't it Driscoll? ... Anderson.

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Now, she wrote up a little... But she hasn't got near everything. The beginning, you see, of Troy. But see, Grandpa Johanson was one of the..… beginners… and there was..… westburg was one. I think that went down on Burnt Ridge. Let's see, who else? Swan Erikson. He was the blacksmith at the time. So, I just can't... There's a book that's written, who you said, by... The Tall Trees.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: The Trees Were Tall?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Trees Were Tall.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: By John Miller?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes. Now, that's interesting. He's got more of interest in that than this other one. That's the Bovill area. Yes. That has more details of that. I knew Bovill. Because he used to come down to dance. These old timers used to kind of horse back around. I call it horse around. Well, this is the language they used at that time. Sometimes you hear this, you horse around. That's what these old timers used to horse around. I think the expression is kind of funny, you know… like Benson.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: You know the Bensons?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: They went to Clara Benson. She married a Hoydon. She's the Clara Hoydon now. Well, when she was a girl, she was home. And Bensons were close to Johansson's right cross. You know, about a mile. So, when I got tired of cultivating that prune orchard up there. Dorothy was baby. She was about a year old. So, I take her and I put the saddle on one of the old legs that I was using for cultivating. And take off over to the neighbor. Well, I take off over to Bensons because I'm Mrs. Benson. So, she'd always have something of interest to talk about, you know. And here was those boys. And they were just flabbergasted here that I was having that baby with me on the saddle. So, when we get in, old Bensons said, well, you sure horse around. And you hear that kind of thing. So, I did little horsing around here. Riding horseback.

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: I lived in the brickyard. That was in 1915. But before that, when he'd come out, he had the homestead there. And he set up the sawmill. So, he saw lumber there for the neighbors around. So, they built their homes.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Did he come out by himself? Did he hook up with his friend in Minnesota and come out?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes. He had the sawmill in Minnesota first. He had a sawmill in Minnesota. And you know, that bird. This is all in this write up on the history of the mural of Troy. How he come out here. It's all in that. So, but he didn't, he started, he didn't put in this big prune orchard up there which helped. A lot of the kids, you know, come over there and pick prunes for us at the time they were ripe. And after he built the dryer up there, you know, then we had to have somebody to help then. Which gave work to just young folks. This sounds like he was pretty enterprising. He had a prune orchard, prune dryer, and a prune orchard. Well, the first prune dryer he had was done, he built that down in Troy. Because he thought it would, it just helped transportation on account of, you know, like horsing around with teams. And wagons to haul them after they're dry. So, he built the prune dryer down there and just hauled the prunes down there. Then it wasn't far to get them out into, you know, commercial, into different stores and to the wholesale house. Because he sold them to the wholesale house. Well then later, in the later years, he thought, well, he'll just build the prune dryer up on the farm. So then, after he did that, he had his prune dryer for sale. Well then, he sold the prune dryer to the Nazarene people for a church. So the Nazarene church is the old prune dryer part of it. Which was a good, did it, a good purpose.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And where was his farm in relation to where that, the prune dryer was set up?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Now, where he had this prune dryer? That was right on the farm, right on the orchard. Oh, I see. Right on the orchard. So we just rolled in, got the prunes right in, and we carried them right into the prune dryer.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Now, did he have the prune, was he doing the prune business at the same time he was doing the sawmill?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes, oh yes, I was going to hold them at the same time. Different people did the different prune. Now, I know when we were up there, when he had this prune sign, I could carry the prunes. And we had some of the Colleen girls, Amelia Colleen, she lives in Troy, and I'm, let's see, she's, oh golly, I can't think of my memory, my offense. See, that shows an ages taken off memory, even though it was good at one time. But Mother always told me I had good memory, but I got it short, short from the shoulder stuff. Which is, she would get him now. Anyway, she was one of the best prickers she had, one of them. She would just, oh, I don't know, she'd just put a 60 pound box in just a few minutes and have them nice and clean… tooth paint… and then we'd wheel them down to the prune dryer and put them in the, for dry, in different, we had to treat them. First treat them and then put them out on 25 pound screens. So by the time we had the crop in, we had about three tons of dried fruit, of dried fruit. And the last ones, that was, I was up on the farm then, and Ed was in Alaska that I took care of. We got three cents a pound for the dried. 25 cents a lug for the green, that's 60 pounds. I just can't get over it. And now when you go to the store and buy a pound of prunes, or a dollar a pound for just a handful.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Well, was three cents a pound, was that a top price at that time?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: At that time, but it was awfully low. You couldn't, if we'd had to hire everything, we couldn't have made anything on it. But I got cheap help. I got some, my brother and some of the kids around the neighborhood, and the Colleen boys were great to help.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: So that after your father-in-law was through running the prune dryer and the prune business, then you and your husband had it?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes, we did run the orchard. And then Ed worked in the clay pit, and getting that out for the factory down in Troy.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: The brick factory?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: The brick factory.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Now, did he also have the brick factory at the same time that he had the sawmill and the prune dryer?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: It was all in the operation. It was all going on, different people, different workers.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: But all at the same time?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: All at the same time. It wasn't year to year, you see. This is all developed. This is what bothers me now if we get a lot of people in here. What have you got to offer them for wages to live on? Where at that time, these people saw something that they could develop to get people to work, as the community was growing. See, these young people had children growing up, and this gave them work without going out of the village. I call it the village, that's the term we use. The pioneer work there. So, instead of you're driving the cars, burning gas, no, you're mobiling around.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: What do you think killed the town of Nora?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Well, it needed to cooperate with Troy and Deary. And it was better for them, just very few people and these people going. They had to go to school, the children, they grew up there to higher school, which education comes first. Then the old people are sitting there by themselves, and they can't carry on just like when they have the family all at home. So, it was logical for them to divide between the other towns, like Troy and Deary and Bovill. When lumber, when logs and lumber had gone out, so they turned that back into farming, which is just as well. Troy benefited, and Deary benefited, and so does Bovill. Moscow, Moscow benefited great. Some say Moscow benefited more than any other place. Yes, they do. And which I like to see individual business. I am not entirely for these big businesses, company businesses coming in. It's competition, but it gives the person, the younger people a little harder start. It's you things, so you want to start a little community store or something that would just make your bread and butter, just a little living. You can't do it because there's too big a competition. I wouldn't be surprised that like Troy and Deary, as Moscow grows, they bring in Sir Roebuck, they bring in Montgomery Ward, pennies will grow up, that's the way it's up in Anchorage now. It cuts out the smaller person that tries to make a living. That's really quite benefit to the community to build it up. It's benefit for the big companies too, it benefits in one way, but it takes away from another. This can be good or it can be serious. I get coming out with the younger people, it's hard for them to start a home.

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: So you get married and you want to buy a home, how can you if you haven't got something you can make a living on? You've got to go into an apartment house, if you haven't got a home, you've got to put up a tent. Whereas when you were growing up in Troy and even when you went to Alaska, it seems like you could make your start. Yes, that's right. If you're willing to put in a little work, a lot of work. Put in some work yourself, you can make it. But you can't do it now. Not the way I see it, because they come in with these big stores and take the big company, operation, even in logging. These big companies have these big trucks, they take away something from these smaller people that have equipment and could do the same work. Even I turn out a little better than I am. Probably I'm a pessimist.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Do you think Troy could ever be like it was when you were growing up there?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: I think so… i think it could. I think there's developments that could be made in one way or the other. I'd like to see that the clay development could be made up a little more stronger in competition with what's there now. It would divide work, help make more jobs for people, for the young folks. There used to be a lot of fruit around the country. But I understand one reason that there is not all the spraying that they've done for wheat and other produce that comes out of the ground kills the fruit trees. So it won't bear. It won't kill them, but the fruit wouldn't bear. Now this was totally done in Brussels, down there by one of the old fellows that had an orchard. So the spraying has cut down the fruit for us. Well I've heard that there was a lot of fowl in this area. Hungarian partridges and different types of birds in such great quantities. You take these Chinese pheasants. I was down in Tennessee with my sister there in time. I said, you know, I think these are so interesting birds, but they're not very interesting for the field. The old hen would come out and fly right at the top when the ring was right and just thrash. And the little fellows would be down underneath picking it up. And they could make streaks right through the fields. Now I don't know if there's enough of those birds that can thrash every week before it's ready to take care of yourself. Anyway I saw this and I thought it was interesting. I thought it was real, you know, that the old hen knew what she was doing. She'd just fly over, you know, and that would thrash the dry wheat when it was dry. The little fellows would be down under there. So some of the birds had to be gotten rid of. Yes, and then after seeding, you know, they'd be able to pick up the seed. That could be a little damaged. But I don't know if that would be too much. Like now we have the coyotes out in the area there. And they used to come around. They had bounty on them. You don't have to go on squirrel poison like we did years ago. And kill them and work on that because it's food for those animals. Then if these coyotes, you know, they feed up on this, they give the trapper a chance to trap these hounds or coyotes for the first. And then they get paid for these kinds. We're getting kind of short on the leather too. So there's another idea, see, that the younger people can go ahead and be a trapper and take care of this. Same thing with the beaver that's so eager now. He's sure been eager out at my place. He's the busiest person out there, I think, because he's dammed up. He's got real good ponds there. But he interferes with my driveway. And I don't appreciate that. He'd move away from there. He could take all the rest that he wanted. But he's interfering with that and letting the water come in and wash out my driveway. So we'll have to see about that. He'll have to move. Somewhere close or someplace he can interfere with that. I think it's so interesting. I see those pictures of Troy and it looks so booming and it looks like there's so many people. And living there now, I many times go up and down the streets and I try to imagine what it looked like. Well, look at the convention they have there. How exciting the people were at that time to get the convention down there.

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And that was a state convention?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes. So, now, we could do that. Here I'm leaving, not in. So I consider myself. But we could do that again. Sure, they could do that again. And there they got the church there, you know, the Lutheran church. They got God's followers there. I don't know if they have a hall in there or not. But the church is very active. They could put on a big feed for a convention there. And if nothing else, they could put up a big tent and have them just like, what's his name?

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Billy Graham?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes. So he goes out there and can't find anything else. He finds an old tent. These are things that the person cooperates. This is what I enjoy in my Anchorage Women's Club. One will bring up something, I mean, oh well, if it doesn't, well, we could change that a little bit. We don't say, no, that's no good. But let's bring up other ideas and see what we come up with. So we put them all together and then we choose our ideas. And this is how we have worked in Anchorage with the city and even with our government. I've been on the forum for the governor different times and it's very interesting to sit there and hear the other song and give your own opinion. Friends like the senior citizens that I'm so interested in. And they're talking this big money and all, pile up every taxpayer has to sneeze on our own and earn money to pay for. And I'm not for all of that extra grant because you've got to pay for it.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And why do it when you don't do the individual any good?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: There is some of it you get. For instance, up there we have the O-Pay, which you've got a big grant for. They rent a big building, pay a big price for that. They have two secretaries to pay them. We buy stuff there for these seniors to come in and play with clay and mud. Or some others want to sit down and play cards or just have a couple of chairs and talk, just gossip and history. Well, I don't feel that I have more, I've got too much to do to go over there and sit down like that. And to me, that money is just wasted that we're paying for this. Most of them, a lot of them, they go there, they think this is great for them. But that's just a few. You have enough benefit from it. No. And then, we're like it was here last year, the fellow that's benefited took off from it and didn't know where he's at. He made a good living, he got the money and all. So, I hope they catch him. So now that we're going to get another grant, and I'm bucking around with everything myself, but I'm just one little part of the gear that I've spoken to this, I don't believe it. But there's, naturally, there's a lot of senior citizens that need help, which I'm for. And there's this food help they have, the grant for, you know, the... Meals on Wheels. Meals on Wheels, and also, and we have a grant for that, and I think that's necessary, because there's so many, they're not able to go down and buy the groceries, so they are not cooked. And I think that's great, whatever goes into that is nutrition. And I think that program is fine. And also, they have a program now that they can, they'll come and go once a week, and they can go out, you know, to a different town, we'll be free now, like way up there, between Palmer and Anchorage, or to Seward, if they wish. But they have to pay a little bit for the ride, and the truck, or the bus come and pick them up. That's good for them, because to get out, it's a different interest, is to get them out of the house. I think that's more benefit to them, than to go in and sit down and play with my outdoors, play cards for themselves. So that program is all right. And I'm doing a lot of just volunteer work, and I think if they're able to go down there, they can join me and go out and volunteer. Things are interesting.

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Don't they have that here, ..., now? Kind of a volunteer, and they have a bus too, don't they, that they pick them up. Well, I think that's good for them. That's one program that's all right. But to have this other is not too good. Now here's one program we have up there, and I'm really happy with that. Now, the people that have lived up there 30 years, and worked on low-scale wages, you know, their income from Social Security isn't enough to meet up with the expenses of today. So we got put in that we gave them a bonus. They get a bonus of $125 a month… i give it… i don't know if she deserves it or not, but I'm getting it too. Of course, I'm doing volunteer work, so I figured that's what I'm getting paid for. $125 a month. But it's such a help to those people. What's on the, there's a lot on the thing. The natives too get it. Although they get an extra bonus too. Now they've got their oil bonus, you know. But they're spending that so wildly too. Putting it into big high-rise buildings in Anchorage. With one of them, they'll understand it's just barely there. And that's the attorney that has really gotten to spend that money to keep up this thing. Well, what I think about that, that you take that same money and build up that village. And help them, just like I feel like the people in Troy. Keep your money there and build it, try and build it up. And if people are coming in, let them help and cooperate with them to build it up. So that they can support themselves. Don't go into a place and say, well now I'm just going moving in there to live off of that community. That's wrong. It's just like me moving from here up to Anchorage. It would be wrong for me to just have lived up there and not put in anything to help the community. And it's the same thing around Troy. I wanted to do my best to help the community. Which my heart's always been in. I think that's interesting what you said about the people that had worked, had been up there for 30 years. And had gotten low social security and now they're getting a bonus. Because it seems like those are the people that did the original work in the area. And of course they worked for low wages because of the times.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Who should deserve it more?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: And also, now these people that get this bonus don't have to be on welfare and get food stamps. They have to use this money for that. And you don't have to feel, you feel proud. You've earned this money. That's right. Now the same thing could be done here. For the person that's lived here in this county. So many years, so the state could get a bonus. Get them off of welfare. Everybody don't like to be on welfare. You know, I don't like that feeling that I was degraded down. That I didn't have to be on welfare. You know, some of the people that I've heard talk that were old timers that like worked for the big logging corporations like Potlatch. It sounded like when they got, they'd worked so many years and then when they got near a time when they were going to have to retire, it seemed like they weren't getting a real fair deal. They were getting fired real early so they wouldn't get too much of a pension.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Or they're still getting low pension.

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: And that doesn't seem right. No, no. There's where I think our politicians could step in too and do something about our state. See, I think that, see now we have some pretty good politicians up there. Tony Diamond, our governor there in the early days, he was real sharp. See, I got my, he recommended me on for the post office. So of course I have people from him too, but he was really wonderful. And Wickersham was too. And we've had some good governors here also. When I was in Washington, I was going to call on church. But I just didn't get time to follow this. Your father and your father-in-law came up. I'm interested in that in the brick factory. I had known there was. You know, to me, there's so many things that could be built up. And all it needs is such a group to get together. Just like we did up there in the earlier days. Just us women, about 20 of us. Like I showed you that picture, we're all old. I don't say old women, but we're seniors. There I can call it seniors. We're between, oh let's say 60 and 90. That's the heritage of these women. But we get together, everybody does something. Put in a suggestion of what to do. Well, with one thing we did, we got, was before the centennial. We went to the city, to the mayor, and said we got that old school house there. And they were going to move it and tear it down.

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: I said, how about getting that to our club? And you have the lot down there, and we'll have it moved down on the lot. And fix it up as a memorial of the old school. And for the teachers that had taught him that school. One of, two of those girls in that picture taught him that building. And it made it very interesting when they get up and talk about the schools. And also the students they had in that school at that time. Which now two of them are judges in Anchorage. So, by doing this, the city gave us the right to put it on the city lot. And we, the women, fixed it up. So this is why, you know, they recommend. Well, now say that, that, say they were to do it in Troy and they were going to resurrect that brick yard.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Now, where was that located? The brick yard? Yeah. Well, I don't know anything about the operation or how they made the bricks or where it was located.

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: It's right where it was at. Where greens happen as you get into Troy. That was the brick yard. It's been sold several times.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Is it near, is it near the city park?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Well, the ball park. Before you go under the bridge, under the railroad bridge. Oh. On the right hand side. Oh, I see. I understand that. That's where it was located.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Now, that's not a brick yard anymore, brick factory anymore, is it? Well, they're making some kind of house brick, aren't they? I know it's called, that's the refractory, isn't it?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yeah, so they're making some. I want to go over there when I'm down there and see what they're doing. Because I'm interested, you know, being stuck, we worked for it and did a lot of work. And Ed was a foreman in there early in 1915. And the Erickson boys, you know, were working for Rootford and Hilding.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Where did your father-in-law come up with the idea to have a brick factory?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Oh, from just like I started out with this blank here, you know. He was on the farm and he had this clay and he tried to make brick and he couldn't make it, you know. It wouldn't dry out for him, this fire brick. So then a friend of his come out, he says, well, you know, you have fire clay, not building brick clay. So then he got the idea of putting up a pug mill right there by the saw mill and burnt brick there. And it proved out. So the pioneers there got brick for their chimneys, fire brick. So there was the first start on that fire brick, the burning. It was right there with one horse, pug mill, and the clay that was there, white clay.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: A pug mill?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: They call it a pug mill where you put this clay into this hopper and then you have to mix it. So, you know, just like you put a horse on a old-fashioned marigold and it'd drop. Well, that's the way that he... And then he fixed up a burner, you know, a burner where they could burn the clay. So he experimented a lot there on the farm before they decided to form a company and build this in Troy.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And what was the name of the company?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Idaho Fire Brick. First it was the White Crown Fire Brick. Well, I have some advertisements he had of them, the bricks patterns that they had. And a fellow by the name of Berg, he was a very good brick man, you know, he had a fireplace man. And they made bricks for these mortuary deals, you know, for cremation and for the railroad for the engines. All of these are patterns in this paper I have that I found in Ed's collection. So it just started because he had that material on his... That's right, it just started because...

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Is that his property from where the Nazarene church sat all the way over to where that brickyard was?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Oh no, no, no. The brickyard, they bought that land and built the brickyard separate after they organized the company. Before it was no company, it was just, you know, grandpa made the brick up there at the farm, right down by the mill where he had the sawmill.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And where was the sawmill located?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Up there on the farm, right up at Nora. Up at Nora. So he had a sawmill at Nora, he had the prunes where the Nazarene church is now. Yes, he had the fire there. And he had the orchard up there on the farm. That was in Nora. Yes, that was in Nora. And then he hauled the prunes down to the dryer and dried them there. He also had the apples, he dried apples at that time too. And then he had the brickyard. That didn't live one horse deal. Right, but he lived in Nora. Yes, on the farm.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Now, did he homestead at all? Did he claim baby? Did he claim his homestead too?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: And then there was the Colleen. And Mrs. Colleen was a relative of Grandma. See, they become a family dealer. And there was Erin Johnson, Mrs. Erin Johnson. I don't know if she was a relative, but anyway, he sent money to Sweden to bring her out to help Grandma work. And that's Elmer Johnson, and Walter Johnson's mother. That's in Troy. And Walter's up here in Mouse. Well, their mother worked for Grandma and he sent for her to Sweden. I don't know, there was some relation there, but I don't know about that. Because we didn't talk about those things, you know. I didn't know too much about the family until the trip I went to Sweden. Then I got to know, and I was kind of surprised, flabbergasted, you know. Just knowing the history line, why hadn't we talked about that before? Just like with my family too, Mother and Dad. Of course, Mother, we never talked more about her mother and father because he was a minister.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: In Norway?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes, I was a minister in the town there. And when you were a minister, you were also the teacher there. And no education in that at all. And then two Mother's sisters were missionaries in Aarhus. One went to China, one went to South America. Well, the one that went to South America developed a fever or whatever, so she dined there to South America. That's on the printer for my time.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: About 1800?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: It was in 1800.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: It was about the middle of the 1800s?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yeah, it was in the middle. It was in the 60s of 1800.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And that's your grandparents?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: That was my aunt, my mother's sister. They're all gone now. And a lot of the second generation is gone. Now when I was back East this last summer, I went to Iowa there and saw some of them. There was a couple of my double cousins, Mother's sister married my father's brother. So they've come, kind of double cousins, but they were so glad to see me. Oh, just hugged me and kissed me and all this. Well, I was getting ready to go on the bus and there was an old lady sitting on the bus. She was looking at all this performance. And so when I got into the bus, what she said, Lady, she said, I think you need a chaperone. Yeah, those boys did that kind of fresh.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Since we're talking about your family, did your parents migrate together from Norway or did your father come first to the United States?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: He come first to Iowa.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Now was he married?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: No, they got married in Iowa.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Was your mother from Norway too?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: From the same town?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: No, no. They were quite a distance. My father was from around Bergen, not far out of Bergen. And Mother was on what they call Etne. That's from Haugesund in that area. I've been there twice. It was interesting. I just wonder why they left that country because it's so beautiful. But at that time, it was just like people leaving Troy during the Depression. There was nothing to live off of. They wanted to venture out to make a living. So they come on to making such big stories on the United States, how wonderful that would be to develop and all that. So this is how they come out. Well, then we had an uncle in Iowa and that's how he come out. He wanted to stay home. So he got a job with the railroad. He sent her mother, so then they got married. Oh, but they did know each other in Norway. Oh, yes.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Was it your father that was in the sailing?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes. My grandfather was a captain and also a ship builder up near Narvik. I can't remember just exactly what the folks say, but that's what he was.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And did he have his own shipping?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes. That's how my father went out. My grandfather took my dad out with him. He was just eight years old then. And you know how it is with kids. They don't want to follow up with your parents' deal. So when he got to be older, he wanted to venture out with other ships and go around the world, which is him, in sailing.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: His father wasn't going around the world?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: No, he was doing more shipping around Norway, Sweden, and Denmark, and Germany. He was just around. It was all sailboats. There were no big boats at that time.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: There were the windjammers?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: The windjammers, what they call them. Something on the sailing boats, they called them.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And so then your father sailed?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes, he sailed on and on. And even when he went with the company as a purser, as a sailor, that was the windjammers too. They went around Cape Horn, South America. They shipped coffee and got from South America and brought it to Norway and Sweden… and what else… and fruits. Then they'd get these colored boys to work. They were good workers. One time he was telling about that they had two colored boys that went with them to Norway on the ships.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: From where?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: From South America… i see… and they'd never seen the coloreds amongst the young people. And they were just scared of them. And so he said, no, they were just sunburnt. No, he didn't. The sunburnt. That Indian kind of, he was quite a joker too, you know. But they stayed there like, you know, so these colored people stayed. So now there's some colored people there. Not very many. I didn't see very many colored people. But there was a few at Ron Bergen when I was there. And they were mostly in the hotel room work, you know, as cooks and work, you know.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: So your father, when he decided then that he no longer wanted to sail, he decided he just wanted to come to America?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes, there was such a, you know, stampede, he called it at that time, going to America because you could make money easier there to support, which was very hard. They spent in Norway, Sweden and Denmark at that time.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Which is about what time?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: In the 1800s. Late 1800s.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Was it a famine? Now is it the same thing that affected your father-in-law?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes, but it was, well this was before because he was older than my father. Johanson was quite big, so that was before. But it affected Sweden quite badly. You've heard of the Alicia, they, let's see, they come on Christmas, you know, the Lucia. That's how that started because a ship from up in the East side of England come in with Christmas supplies for the food and that. And a girl come in there with these candles on her, you know, because there's no lights to light, you know, the way. And when the ship come in. So since they had carried this on as a legend, it's a nice one. Oh yes. I've seen pictures of this. And now in Anchorage we carry this on every year, the Lucia. And we select, you know, the queen, whatever you call her, the girl to be the lizard and the wand. And she's dressed up, you know, with a white robe and the lights. This year we didn't use candles, we used these little flashlights, you know, that you see in the room. And so it was more safe, you know, for fire and that. She didn't have to be rolled quite so, be careful. And they looked like, you know, burning candles. So the change didn't make too much because they liked to keep their original thing. The tradition. There's so many legends like that. Just like Denmark and Sweden, you know, have this queen, you know, out there driving her for her oxen. You know, when Sweden said that the queen of Denmark could toil that piece of ground, soil, between Sweden and Denmark. Sweden would give her that ground. Well, she didn't know how to do it, but she took her four sons and hooked them up as oxen and toiled the land. So Sweden had to give that piece of land to Denmark. You know, fairy tales. That's just about as funny as I am. I struck it in Jerusalem when I was there.

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: I asked the Jewish lady, I said, where is the mountain that Noah's Ark landed on? She said, well, that's a fairy tale. I don't know, sorry. Oh, I can't find it because the Jews, you know, they have their own. It's bizarre, you know, you get to meet up with those funny things. Oh, yes. Oh, yes. Well, I think I understand how your father left Norway because of hard times. That's it.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: What brought him to Iowa?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Well, he had an uncle there. Oh, I see. And he had written to his uncle and he said, well, he'll go and see. But he liked it quite well. And of course, mother was coming out and she wanted him to quit the sailing. She didn't want to sail beyond, away from home for it. So he had to sign it. So he went back to Norway, you know, on this ark of this. And then that's when they decided he'd come back. He had already gotten the promise of this job that he could get with the railroad. And so then after he'd gotten the job, then he sent for her and got married. It seems like that would be hard to leave your whole family and your whole way of life and come to a new country. Yes, it wasn't easy. I can see mother talk about it. And, you know, travel was so inconvenient at that time. She said that coming across oceans, people were sick and it wasn't the accommodation like it is up today. Far, she said it wasn't. But anyway, she was glad they'd come and then her sisters come. And then grandma passed away, you see, and grandpa, you know. So there was no ties left for them in those years. They felt that they had to just stay there, which I could see too. Just now, my parents are gone up at Troy. There's no one there living about relatives, you know, there. So just to stay there for my relatives wouldn't be my drawing there. But it's because it's the community I like myself. Therefore, I like to be there and not give it up. And so it was with them and leaving, they had no time, but they liked this better, you know. They were helping in Iowa. And that was a new country too then, not too old. Any railroad building and getting work on the railroad. So this is what your father, of course, he was kind of aggressive too. He wanted to be there where he could make a headway. So he started, you know, on the railroad section for them. Then he got the contract to get coal and deliver it to the Indians. He called it coal bunkers. They had the coal bunker, big building, where they come in with the coal and then you have to fill these. It was a contract on them. So then, after he'd been out here, and just in here, he'd like to make that change.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: How did he get out here to see this part of the country?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: He come to Moscow. Then from there, they had to hike it out. Did he just, he was living in Iowa. Yes, but he come out here in 1901, and just to see the country.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: With your mother?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: No, no. He left us behind. He just decided he wanted to come out and see it. Yes.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Had he heard about it? Yes. I wonder what he'd heard.

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Well, the papers were telling about the Weyerhaeuser, or the Paul Bunyan, they call it, you know, from the scouts. Those people were moving out west and they come. All the good timber and that, sawmills going in, and farming, just homesteads, always bragging in order to do that today too. It was more really than it turns out to be, but this turned out pretty good. So he decided to come out on top of that. So then, the railroad was being built between Pullman and Troy, or had just about been finished at that time. But the way he said they had a livery team that they took to go out to Troy to see the timber and all that, where they went. But they didn't take the train, they had a livery team. That was with this Tobias that was here at that time. And he was one of them that went out. So they organized and had set up this mill there on this flat. And that's where that mill started. And then they called it the farmer's mill because they sawed the lumber for those pioneers so they could rebuild their homes.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And where was that sawmill in relation to where your home was with your family?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: About two miles from where we lived. Well, we lived on the first Burnt Ridge there. So that was about a mile and a half, something like that, away from the mill.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And the mill was where?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Down on Camp Creek, they called it. So then as soon as Father got a house built down there, we moved from Burnt Ridge down to the place so we'd be right down there. So Mother could take care of it, she took charge of the mess house. Then after, you know, we had help at first. Then she had to have somebody look after us youngsters. And that's how come dance up the idea of getting a tutor and going in there and help us with education. Because that would come first.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Well then how old were you when you started school? When you no longer had a tutor up until that time?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: I had a tutor then. I should have been a boy. I was always on the side with Dan with the horses and out in the lumber. So he always called me Nels.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Nels?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Thomas Nels, I should have been a boy.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Well you worked in the saw mill didn't you?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes, uh huh.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: How old were you when you started that work?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: About twelve.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And what were you doing?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Taking off from the planer mills, you know, the moldings, light lumber, you know, it was easy. He didn't put me on the thing heavy. But so that, and be careful so we didn't let it bend or break, you know, because they were easy to break. So then we had to pile them up and tie them up and tie them. Of course he did that because he had a certain way of doing things. It had to be just so. So that he wouldn't break and pack. And then he'd haul that to Moscow here, you know, to the standard lumber company.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Did any other women work at the mill?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: No, uh huh.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Just you?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Just me. And that was done. We didn't do it when we had the crew. This was in the summertime really after the main sawing was done. And the lumber was dried when the crew, see it was just seasonal work for most, like the crew you saw there on the picture. So when the sawing was done and that the lumber was drying and then after we kids got older, well then we were the ones that had to be the crew with him. Because he run the planer mill and the light mill. And one of my relatives, Oswald, he was the engineer. So he stayed. So it was kind of the planning then at that time. You said that there were Indians in this area when you... Well that was in the beginning, uh huh. They come down there and they can't. They had their daylight scared on them. Because it would be very good if the Indians could take you. So one night they were coming up close and I crawled under the bed. I said they'd have to look. But I think it's foolish to look to scare children. People, I don't care how bad they are, if they were, it's not good for them because it kind of sticks and stays with you. You know, and you don't think it should be done.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Can you remember, did you have much interaction with the Indians?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Quite a bit because Dad did buy, or they bought lumber from Dad. And I had a picture with Chief Joseph, who said, well Dad has a picture with Chief Joseph. And they were up dealing with them. And the Indians come out to Tennessee and my brother-in-law was ranting line from the Indians down there. See they had quite big lines. They'd run down there and down them they'd rim rocks. So we just got in contact with them that way. And they're no different than we are to you. Not at all.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: What use did they have for the lumber?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Well, it was that shop lumber they wanted. They shopped around for shop lumber and trading horses too. Dad had quite a few horses and he traded. That's how Chief Joseph knows from. They had horses that he bought.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: They were building houses?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Well, they were built down there on the Lapwai. Oh, I see. On the reservation.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And Chief Joseph himself did come up here?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes, he was up here himself. Up to Troy. Up to the Kamehameha. And then they were down to him and Dad met with them down in Lewis and Madison. That's where he and my brother-in-law they all had their picture taken down there. I'd like to see if I can get a hold of one of those. I had one but my sister-in-law, or my sister-in-law, had done it. It would be kind of interesting. As I recall, now he's Chief Joseph. I know I've seen where Chief Joseph is buried in NSPL in Washington. And I knew he had been separated from his tribe. Yes, I don't know. But you see he was first buried out at Enterprise. See at Lake Bay, that's where he wanted to be. Isn't he still there? I hadn't heard that day moved him. This is young Chief Joseph. Oh, young Chief. This is the old man. I wonder if it's the same for the one that led the flight into Canada. That's the same Joseph that I'm talking about, not his father. Oh, no, this is different then. But old Chief Joseph was the one then. He was real old at this time. No, not his. That was Joseph and then his father was also Joseph. And the younger Joseph, as I understand it, was the one that led the Indians, tried to get them into Canada. And he's the one that surrendered. His father was dead by that time. Yes, I remember when he died.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: The oldest Joseph or the youngest?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes, that was back in, let's see, 1913, 1914. That's when Chief Joseph, who led the Indians, tried to lead them to Canada died. Oh, well then it could be. I'm not so clear. I can't remember everything. Only I know that their father had contact with them. I'm sure it's the same Joseph that we're talking about. It probably is. I just can't. But I know that they used to come up. But the group was only once that I can remember come up and camped. But Chief Joseph himself, there was horses that they had bought or traded with him. Something about horses. And so was my brother-in-law. He was a great trader.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Were they easy to deal with?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Oh, we thought they were very nice to deal with. That we couldn't find any. I didn't think they were any different than us. And there was Santee, a girl, Del Sago, a native girl, Indian girl. I just loved her. I thought she was just beautiful. And Irma, there was two girls there. They lived down there, Genesee, across to my sister's and husband's place down there. The girl, I talked to her this morning because they were going to come up and get me. I said, no, I won't be through today. I'll just wait until tomorrow. But you see, the little part, there was all the Indian land. Genesee down over there. Not all of it. I guess there's some that some said. But I know they rented from the Indians down there. And I think my native still rents some from the Indians down there. But you can see the difference on them now. Oh, there's a few. Oh, yes, the night before last I went to the Liferay and Lewiston Junior ballgame. Oh, I don't know. One of them had greats. You could tell he was the coach. But there is some difference between the two kids. It's just that they own so much land. You know, in part of the country that then was opened up for settlement by the immigrants, the white people. I just wondered how much the Indians feel seeing that land just taken away from them. Well, I don't know. It has to be developed. There has to be development. And when there is a development, it benefits the other person. See, like the Indians, they benefited by it. They got their school. They got their hospitals, you know, down in Liferay. They were benefited indirectly, even though you had to give to receive.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: You don't think that they were led a better life before this was opened to a white settlement?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: I don't think so. Because they opened up to more convenience, a better living. It's just what they wanted to themselves. If they all wanted to keep on the tepees, that was there. But they didn't. They wanted a better living. So, I think if it comes in... But I don't think that people should fight for everything, you know, to gain it. I think it could be agreed upon and discussed. And then accept one way or the other. Just like we get into fight arguments sometimes, these women and I, you know. But you've got to take the best suggestions out of it. And what's the best benefits?

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: For everyone.

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: For everyone. Consider that. And so it was, I think, in older days too. With the Indians. I think they might feel that they have been let out. Through, just through our talk and paperwork. You know, writing and that. They could. And they are no different than we are. There are some greedy and some willing to give and some are not. And you see all these Indian fighting stories. I don't think we should even put that out for these younger people. Because life is like that for fighting. Why put it out so you learn more about it? Like these little fellas. I was going to one place and I had gotten a little BB gun. And he's punching me. He yelled at me and said, shoot you. Surrender, he says. Well, they learned that soon enough. They shouldn't have it when they're two and three years old. I don't agree with that. Do you?

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: No not at all. To learn how to be violent.

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yeah, you learn how to be violent. You learn that soon enough to win your fight for life.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Did you say that, where was the wood that your father was manufacturing in the saw mill going to? Timber?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yeah. Well, that went up here to Moscow and to Spokane for, they call it shop lumber. See, moldings and door casings… i see… and then he made these curved moldings up in the ceilings. They were from the clear lumber. They call it shop lumber. And so they call this shop material. And this was bundled and sent up here to Moscow and in Spokane. I can't recall that we sent any to Lewiston, but I think that was in and around Troy and the neighbors when they were building.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Well, where did most of the lumber that people were using to build their homes within Troy coming from? Any one particular saw mill?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: No, but they patronized all of the mills, it seemed like, because they patronized my father's out there. And they patronized a lot to Moscow here because he was interested with the standard lumber company. Being sent, his partner was with them. So that gave a good outlay for them. So they would either haul that up here with a team of horses or ship it from Troy on the cars. That's why he had that spur down by the railroad tracks there. That sewerage clank, that's that.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Was Vollmer in operation when your family came out to Troy? Or was he gone by then, J .P… vollmer?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: No, he was still there, I think. I was so young then, you know, I was older, about ten. You know, at that age you don't pay much attention to anything going around, only your home. Because I'd known that Troy was named Vollmer. Yeah, well that was the name after L .P., you know, because he had, I think he was the one that had the first saw mill,… i believe. He was the one who I've talked to, and from my father. And then of course he was interested in this timber that was on the ridges around there, which was beautiful timber. I really, in my memory now, I miss that timber. You go around Burnt Ridge where you had that beautiful tall pines, and they were just nice, they made beautiful lumber. And they were not small either, even though they were tall. They were, someone was around three feet across. That is the boards. Now, out there at the home, the counter there is just one board. It's not grooved, it's just one board out of one tree. See, the width of it. And this is why I'm kind of sentimental with it. Oh, I understand.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Well, was Troy called Troy when you first got there, or was it Vollmer?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: No, it was Vollmer.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: And do you remember why they changed the name?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Well, it was something to do with Vollmer, too, you know. He left, and he was a little bit greedy, I understood, from the old timers. Of course, he was pretty good. He loaned these people money, and then when they couldn't pay, he got their places. And that didn't, they didn't approve of this exactly, but what else could they do? So he made himself a pretty good wealthy man. And then, I don't know if he moved to Lewiston or somewhere else, I think that's where he moved to Lewiston. And then everybody else, it took over. And it's been going on as Troy ever since. And the community, I think, has been wonderful. They've kept it growing. And now it's still, I'm really proud of it. That's why I don't want to let go up down there. I understand. Well, you know, your father became Justice of the Peace in 19... 18. 18.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Did he run for that office, or?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: I don't remember if he was appointed or if he ran for it. I wasn't paying any attention. I was married by that time. Oh, I see. I was married in 1915.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Were you still living in the area?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Oh, I never went out of the area until we went to Alaska. I see. We lived down on the Johanson Farm, and did the farming there on the fruit trees, the fruit, let's say. That's what's going on about all those fruit trees and fruit. And that was kind of nice because it gave the neighbors right close to them their little picking jobs for picking the fruits.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Well, now when you and your husband then moved to the Johanson Farm, was the brick factory still going, the brick plant still going?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes. That's the home. Yeah, it started in 1913. And see, we lived in Troy, and he worked at the factory at the brickyard. But then his folks wanted us to move out on the farm so they could be out there. So they were out there with us. And that's why they gave me a chance to work out in the field. So that's when I was cultivating the orchard, and Ed and the CT could make us some money. So he worked in the clay pit. And then in the fall, of course, he'd have to help with the drying of the fruit, digging of the potatoes and all. And back then, we had quite a few potatoes one year, but there was no price there. So they were just about a total loss, except that between Ed's father and Ed, they made that potato mill, so we made potato starch. And so the potato starch got enough to pay for the potatoes. At least we didn't have to buy gunnysacks to put the potatoes in, because the potatoes were less than the sacks cost.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Well, did you have then that brick factory until you went to Alaska?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Well, that was all recently they sold the factory.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: At that time during the Depression?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes, at that time. The company, the Idaho Crown Factory. The Idaho Crown and Brick, I think they called it at that time. You know, that's a few years. I have a painting, but I want to go up there and see now, because they built the fire kilns to fire the brick. And they stood there for many years, the kilns there. You know, it's good for a concern, a company to change. It's good for them to sell out and that other people get their money. And then let somebody else start over again and see what development they can make for the benefit of the community. It's good, that change is good. It's good to change a job. So this is what I look at. It's good for a community to change. Sometimes you don't change for the good, but anyway you try. And this plant up there has been good for Troy. It's helped quite a few of the young folks for getting a job. And that way I hope that they can continue on. I hope they can build. I hope they can add something else to that plant to hire more people, to have more employees. Each employee means at least $50 a week to a community. That is to your town. Because they have to spend their money. They have a car, they've got to buy gas and oil. They've got to have something to eat. So you can say the least they would spend is around that. And this is what the community needs. They need development and they need somebody real excited in planning. Which I think Troy's always said that. Otherwise it would be just like Howell and Dierion, or not Dierion, Joel and Howell. See they were little towns up along between here and Moscow. And if they can keep, you know, they could, the chambers of commerce and a good contact and good planning, they can still grow up on the map. I feel.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: What were the towns of Joel and Howell, what was their purpose and existence?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Well it was for the farmers, the post office, at that time being horse and buggy days. Like some of them always said, they were always said to horse around with horses hauling. And that's the same thing back east too, where we come from. Now Iowa, you know, they have over 90 counties. They don't need that. But it was during the years back, you see, where they didn't have the convenience of transportation. So they made counties and courthouses to send them. That made jobs. That was jobs they created. Of course now it's just like Troy. They send all their popcorn to Alaska in the army. That's what I told them about, they run the tour around. I said, well these people from Iowa, you know, they've been very good. They send all their popcorn up to Alaska so they don't have hardly any left. Iowa and Iowa. You know, just quite a few soldiers come up there and colonels. So this is why I had to bring the popcorn in. Well, you jubble and how it wouldn't be big enough that you would go there. No, no. We'd stop there with the team if we drove to Moscow. The only way we could go was either on the train or drive up. We made several, quite a few trips up to Moscow. I got very seriously ill when I was home. I was only 14 years old. They had to take me to the hospital right in the afternoon. They hung me and I should have taken me up in a buggy. They had to make a bed and put me on the bed. The doctor was with me. Take me to Moscow. And Carithers was the hospital in. Carithers Hospital. So there's where I was operated on. I was just, oh my gosh, I can't even think what year that was in. I had obstructions of the large intestines. So they had to operate besides starting in Grangeville. I lived quite a while. At that time you weren't too serious. You didn't think too serious about any illness. You just had a summer complaint or you had colic. So that's all I had, but it ended up into something more than that. So I had my illness when I was just a youngster.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Was it frightening to have to go to a hospital at that time?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: I was too sick to think about it. Because with that obstruction, everything, even water, when I drank that would retreat. So I was too sick to know whether, I wasn't thinking about anything. And I didn't know anything until after I was operated on, kind of come to. But I was just 14 then.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: That wasn't a very big hospital, was it?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: No, but it was a nice hospital. It still is there. It has a dome where they have the operating room.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Is that where you were operated on?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes. Dr. Carithers and Dr. Wick and Dr. Olsen were the doctors.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Three doctors and nurses too?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes, I can't remember the nurses now because that's a few years back.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: Now that wasn't originally built as a hospital, was it?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Yes, it was a hospital at that time. It was a nice little hospital.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: It has that big porch, you know, so when I got sold they put me in the wheelchair and they'd wheel me out on this and I thought to myself, why did I have to scrape to go out there and see those horses and buggies go by?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
words: Well, there was a few cars there too at that time. I'll sit up and sit in the, oh golly, 1910. Someone's sitting there. They had electricity there, so they were doing away with the street lights, you know, the lamp lighters. That was something that was interesting to me, these gas lights that they had to light. In Spokane, they had those too. I just could watch those and I would watch the lamp lighter. He was always humming, singing, coming to light those lights. Because we stayed there for about a week in Spokane before we moved down here to Moscow. And the first place we went was called then the Pleasant Home. It was kind of a rooming house at that time, so we stayed there until Father could get us organized to bring us down to a birth rate. And Mother got sick, she had pneumonia there at that time, so we had to stay. And my sister was a baby, so it was up to me to be a babysitter and help with that.

speaker: Rachel Foxman
words: How did you come out with your family to Idaho? What was your means of transportation?

speaker: Nellie Johanson
